topic: Anchoring: the first number you see
title: The Pricing Trick Stores Use on You
voiceover: Why do stores show you a big number first? In 1974, Tversky and Kahneman had volunteers watch a wheel spin to a random number. Then they asked what percentage of African countries are in the United Nations. People who saw the number 10 guessed about 25 percent. People who saw 65 guessed about 45 percent. A random, irrelevant number pulled their estimates toward it. This is called anchoring. Anchors matter in negotiations too. In three experiments, whoever made the first offer got a better outcome. But when the other side thought about their own alternatives, the first-offer advantage disappeared. So when someone makes the first offer, think about your own target and their alternatives before you answer. Tomorrow: why do you forget why you walked into a room?

description: Why do stores show a big number first? In a classic experiment, a random number changed people's estimates, a result known as anchoring. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131. Source: Galinsky, A. D., & Mussweiler, T. (2001). First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 657-669.
accuracy_note: Figures are medians from the original wheel-of-fortune experiment (25 and 45). Anchoring is a robust finding, but effect size varies by task. Galinsky & Mussweiler studied simulated negotiations. The video does not claim that stores' 'original prices' work exactly this way; it presents the lab result and the negotiation research.
